Compulsory

kum-PUL-suh-ree — stress the PUL; a compulsory rule pulls you in whether you like it or not. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Compulsory is required by a law, rule, or authority, leaving no choice about whether to do it.

Wearing a seatbelt is compulsory in nearly every state, no matter how short the drive.

Worked Example

A school announces that attendance at the fire drill is required for every student and staff member, with no exceptions for any reason. Anyone who skips it faces a serious penalty.

A rule that allows absolutely no exceptions and carries a real penalty for skipping it is compulsory. Unlike 'recommended,' which merely suggests, compulsory means there is no legal choice in the matter.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

mandatory: required by a rule or law

obligatory: required as a duty or by rule

required: needed or demanded by a rule

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

optional: available to choose or not choose

voluntary: done by free choice, not forced

Where it sits · how impossible it is to skip — recommended → compulsory → unavoidable

recommended vs. compulsory: A recommended action is only advised — you can skip it without punishment — while a compulsory one comes with real consequences for skipping it.

unavoidable vs. compulsory: Unavoidable is stronger than compulsory: a compulsory rule is imposed by an authority, but something unavoidable cannot be escaped no matter what anyone decides.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — com-

prefix — com-: together, intensive (Latin)

root — -puls-

root — -puls-: to drive, to push (Latin)

suffix — -ory

suffix — -ory: relating to (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin compellere meant 'to drive together, to force.' Something compulsory is imposed with force — you are driven or pushed to do it, with no real choice.

Use the root in a new word: propel

Use the root in a new word: propel: The wind was strong enough to propel the small sailboat across the bay.

Word Choice
